second_extractor_value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Descriptive case-study findings show that although the 2014–2015 drought reduced Paraíba do Sul minimum flow from 190 m3/s to 110 m3/s without interrupting bulk water production at the Guandu ETA, peripheral municipalities suffer chronic hydrosocial scarcity driven by CEDAE's centralized management model, planning/investment deficits, ~40% system water losses, incomplete storage/distribution networks, and operational prioritization of core municipalities (Rio de Janeiro 98% residential network coverage in 2010; Niterói 100%) and industrial users (REDUC petrochemical complex; Queimados Industrial District receiving 200 L/s) over outlying residential districts. In the Eastern Imunana/Laranjal System (6,200 L/s produced vs. 10,900 L/s demand; 4,700 L/s deficit), 2010 coverage was 80% in São Gonçalo (~150,000 people unserved) and 27% in Itaboraí (29% via CEDAE in 2014). In the Western Guandu/Lajes/Acari System (52,400 L/s produced vs. 56,000 L/s demand in 2015; 3,600 L/s deficit), network coverage fell in Duque de Caxias from 69% (2000) to 63% (2010) and in Nova Iguaçu from 81% to 76%, and connected Baixada Fluminense districts receive water only 2–4 days per week via manual switchovers.
comment: Qualitative/institutional case study using descriptive secondary census and engineering data without inferential statistical estimation. Headline finding is that peripheral water deprivation is socially and institutionally constructed rather than caused by bulk drought scarcity alone.

second_extractor_value: Descriptive coverage & disparities: Across urbanized Brazilian localities (>=50% urban), household central water connection coverage rose from 51% in 1970 to 89% in 2000 (51% to 92% in the constant sample of 258 localities), and full service (electricity, central water, and central sewer) rose from 25% to 49%; in 1980, only 61% of small (1-2 room) houses vs. 86% of large (6-7 room) houses had a central water connection (17% vs. 54% for full service), and in 1991 unweighted central water coverage was 57% for small (1-3 room) houses vs. 89% for large (7-9 room) houses, with households not owning the land under their homes worst served. Strategic municipal under-servicing (1991 small-house central water share, mean 0.77): With urban-area fixed effects and inverse-density weights, rival localities' water servicing has a strategic reaction slope of beta = -0.43 in lagged OLS and beta = -0.53 in spatial MLE (-0.69 OLS and -0.59 MLE with equal weights), meaning a 1 percentage point increase in rival localities' small-house water servicing reduces own-locality small-house water servicing by ~0.45 percentage points; moving from lowest to highest locality income and size quintiles raises servicing by 0.48 (48 percentage points) before interaction, but the top-income by 4th/5th-size quintile interaction reduces this gain by 0.16 (16 percentage points), and marginal income and scale effects become negative in large, rich localities in the 23-urban-area subsample (effects vanish in 1991 large-house and 2000 post-democratization small-house counterfactuals). Impact on 1991-2000 locality household growth (N = 351 MCAs in 55 urban areas, mean growth 0.40): Instrumenting 1991 small-house central water servicing with porous geology and insolation (first-stage partial F ~ 13) reverses biased negative OLS estimates to +0.74 in 2SLS (+0.77 with shorter instrument list; +0.78 with river/altitude instruments; p < 0.10) and ~+0.8 in LIML (significant at just over the 5% level), where a 1 SD (0.21) increase in small-house water servicing raises decade household growth by 0.17 (and a 1 SD reduction lowers 2SLS low-educated household growth by 0.17, with a similarly large positive IV effect on high-educated household growth at just over the 5% level). Using the share of untitled houses with central water yields weak instruments (partial F = 6.2; OLS -0.16, LIML 1.82, SE = 2.22, insignificant). Rent hedonics (1980): Central water connection commands a 12% rent premium in Sao Paulo and 23% in Rio de Janeiro; central sewer commands 9% and 18% premiums over no connection.
